text:
End of an era.

After 3 good years on Framer, we moved @designme to our own stack.

Framer got us far, and I'd still recommend it for a lot of teams.

But the more we grew, the more we needed control: over the code, structure and speed of testing and shipping new things.

So, we rebuilt everything from scratch in Astro.

In May, our last redesign took me 4 weeks and roughly 300 hours to create 41 pages.

This one: 228 pages in 4 days. The speed is just unmatched.

116 old URLs mapped, 43 redirects, 0 broken links.

20 case studies, 19 articles, 4 free tools, light and dark mode, and a design system that finally makes sense.

The best part: the whole site runs in Claude now.

New page, copy change, quick fix? We ask, review, and ship. No waiting on someone to open an editor. And if I need something visual, I jump into Figma, mock it up, and ship with an MCP.

It's the same setup we now build for our clients (which is exactly why we had to run our own site on it first).

Really proud of the team and how fast we're moving now.

DesignMe 2.0 is live ↓

text:
Good design with AI is mostly noticing what's off.

I must have prompted Claude 60 or 70 times today and almost none of it was building new stuff.

I'm working on a side project, and Claude builds the pages and components fast, but the styles it creates aren't consistent with each other, so I spent most of the day fixing the small things that don't match.

None of these look like a big deal on their own, but together they make a product feel cheap, and people can pick up on it even if they can't tell you why.

Everyone has the same AI tools now, so people who know what good looks like can get there 10x faster than a year ago.

AI builds what you ask for, so you need to know what to ask for, and that comes from years of noticing when something's 2px off.

text:
'Why spend $8-12.5K a month on design when you can hire someone.'

I asked one founder to run me through their maths on a call last week.

One senior product designer in-house, salary, equity, benefits, recruiter fee, up to three months to hire, at least one more to get up to speed. Then a dev to build what they make, and someone to manage both.

On the other hand, the retainer covers a project manager, a designer and a developer from the first week, with the option to pause when the roadmap slows down.

No surprise a retainer comes out cheaper by a wide margin.

I've had a similar conversation on a bunch of our onboarding calls this year, so I fed the transcripts into Claude and asked what the clients said they were paying for.

- A team that starts on day one
- Design and build from the same people, no handoff
- Zero hiring, onboarding or management overhead
- Predictable monthly output they can plan a launch around
- Someone senior who understands their business by month two

Most startups don't see $8k as a design cost.

They see it as the cheapest way to have a product team before they can afford one.

Most designers skip this because it feels spammy. No one cares.
